title: CR-2 only structurally fixed: data layer never injects Order.price, decodeBidPrice still wrong
description: Iter-2 added an optional Order.price field so computeMarketStats can prefer an injected price over the broken decodeBidPrice bit-decode. However, the production data layer never populates that field. traverseBigVector pushes Order objects with only order_id/quantity/filled_quantity/status — no price. The chain Order struct does not carry price (per chain-shape.md line 130-131); the captured price lives on the companion order_info::OrderPlaced event. The fix would require querying OrderPlaced events and joining them by order_id to inject price into each Order before computeMarketStats runs. Verified math against the captured pair (order_id=12377783720203182843884075, real price=671000): the iter-2 decodeBidPrice still computes id/2^64=671000 then U64_MAX-671000 = 18,446,744,073,708,880,615 (~1.84e19), then loses precision to 18446744073708880000 when cast to Number. Bid prices on a real sandbox will be wrong by ~14 orders of magnitude, exactly the iter-1 critical defect.
impact: Once a real bid order exists on the sandbox, midPrice = (bestAsk + bidGarbage)/2 is dominated by the garbage bid, spread is hugely negative or astronomically positive, and depth at +/-1% from a garbage mid collapses to 0. AC1.4's bestBid<=mid<=bestAsk invariant fails. Tests pass tautologically because marketStats.test.ts uses the same broken bid-encoding builder and dataLayer's T-014 fixture has empty books. The 'fix is in place but untriggered' shape is more dangerous than the iter-1 stub — it looks fixed.
recommendation: In dataLayer.ts, fetch order_info::OrderPlaced events alongside the BigVector traversal and build an order_id -> price map. In traverseBigVector (or in a post-pass), set order.price from the map for every order whose id appears. Add a regression test that constructs an Order with only the captured order_id and asserts computeMarketStats throws or surfaces 'unknown' rather than silently using the bit-decoded value. Alternative: have decodeBidPrice throw when price > realistic max (e.g. > 10^15) so the silent-failure mode at least crashes loudly.

title: fetchPoolStats silently degrades to empty book on malformed RPC response (no shape validation)
description: If sui_getObject returns an envelope whose content.fields is missing/null (e.g. object exists but is a different type, or content was not requested), extractFields returns null. resolvePoolInnerFields returns null. fetchPoolStats falls through to the default-empty PoolInnerState (line 336). buildPoolInnerState similarly degrades: if the resolved fields lack a 'book' key, bookFields becomes {}, asksId/bidsId become '', traverseBigVector returns []. There is no thrown error in any of these branches. The user sees a card with all sentinels ('—') even when the failure is structural (e.g. the deployed package has changed shape). This is the same silent-failure pattern iter-1's CR-1 was a maximally-bad case of — iter-2 reduces the surface area but does not close it. RPC errors with non-2xx HTTP would also slip past: rpc() does not check response.ok before calling response.json().
impact: AC1.1 is satisfied (no runtime error), but the user cannot distinguish 'pool truly idle' from 'shape parse failed.' Operators will misdiagnose sandbox restarts as quiet markets. The H-2 cluster from iter-1 (issue results discarded with no shape validation) is partially carried forward.
recommendation: In rpc() add `if (!response.ok) throw new Error(\`${method} HTTP ${response.status}: ${await response.text()}\`)`. In resolvePoolInnerFields and buildPoolInnerState, throw an actionable error when the expected field set is absent rather than returning a degraded shape. fetchPoolStats can then let the error propagate; App.tsx's allSettled already surfaces per-pool failures in the alert banner.

title: fetchFills cross-pool window contamination: a non-target pool's old event halts our pagination
description: H-1 was 'fix the per-pool filter so we don't sum other pools' volume.' Iter-2 adds `if (ev.poolId !== poolId) continue;` before timestamp checking, which correctly excludes other pools from the accumulator and from `crossedWindow`. Good. However, the related cross-pool concern is that newer Sui pages may interleave events from many pools at high volume; if our target pool's events are sparse, the 50-event page may contain only N events for our pool and (50-N) for others. The early-stop `if (collected.length >= MAX_FILLS) break;` only fires when WE have accumulated 50, so we keep paginating — fine. The `if (crossedWindow) break;` only fires when one of OUR events is older than 24h — fine. So the pure correctness is preserved. The medium-severity concern is throughput: a sparse pool with active competitors can cause O(N_pages) calls per refresh. Not a critical defect; mitigated by the 50-event page cap and the 24h horizon.
impact: Performance under contention rather than correctness. Worst case: 50 paginated calls per pool per 20-second refresh tick, which is ~3 RPC calls/sec sustained per pool. Probably acceptable on a localnet sandbox.
recommendation: Optional: add a hard pagination cap (e.g. max 10 pages per fetchFills call) to bound the worst-case latency. Surface a warning if the cap fires.

title: Versioned->PoolInner traversal is untested: T-014 fixture takes the flat-book early-return branch
description: resolvePoolInnerFields has two cases: (1) the response already has a 'book' field — return directly; (2) descend through inner.fields.id.id -> suix_getDynamicFields -> sui_getObject -> wrapperFields.value.fields. The T-014 fixture always returns case (1), so the entire case (2) traversal — which is the only path that runs against a real sandbox — is uncovered by tests. The chain-shape capture at notes/chain-shape.md Step 3 shows the value-fields wrapper at content.fields.value.fields, which the code reads as wrapperFields['value']?.['fields']. RPC-returned value typically nests under `{ fields: {...}, type: '...' }`, but this depends on the RPC's pre-decoding behavior, which has been brittle across Sui versions. Without a test against a captured Versioned response, a Sui RPC change in the value-shape (e.g. value comes back as raw rather than parsed) would silently produce empty books with no test failure.
impact: The production-only data path has zero test coverage for the dominant traversal branch. A Sui RPC behavior drift would manifest as 'all cards empty' with no actionable signal.
recommendation: Add a fixture in tests that captures a real (or realistically-shaped) Versioned wrapper response and walks resolvePoolInnerFields case (2) end-to-end. The captured shape is already in chain-shape.md Step 1-3 — promote it to a JSON fixture under tests/fixtures/ and consume it from a new test asserting the asks/bids BigVector ids are correctly extracted.

title: cachedPackageId race: empty-string packageId silently used if fetchPoolStats fires before loadManifest resolves
description: main.tsx defines deps.fetchPoolStats as a closure over cachedPackageId (initially ''). It then reassigns deps.loadManifest to a wrapper that sets cachedPackageId after the upstream loader resolves. App.tsx awaits deps.loadManifest before calling deps.fetchPoolStats, so under normal flow cachedPackageId is populated. However, two latent footguns: (1) the periodic-refresh effect in App.tsx runs fetchPoolStats without re-loading the manifest; if the sandbox restarts and emits a new packageId, the SPA will keep calling the old packageId until manually restarted (sparkline freezes silently). (2) Any future refactor that calls fetchPoolStats independently of the App lifecycle (e.g. a test harness, a debug button) would silently get '' as packageId, leading to suix_queryEvents being filtered to a non-existent module that returns zero events — same silent-failure shape as iter-1 CR-1.
impact: Under sandbox restart mid-session (a documented sandbox behavior per chain-shape.md friction notes), the SPA's polling will silently stop reflecting reality. AC1.5 freshness fails without any UI signal.
recommendation: Pass packageId explicitly into the fetchPoolStats closure on each call by sourcing it from a state slot that is repopulated on every periodic refresh tick. Or: have App.tsx reload the manifest as part of the polling cycle and feed packageId through props rather than a module-level cache. Or: log a console.warn once when cachedPackageId is '' on a fetchPoolStats call.

title: rpc() does not check response.ok; non-2xx responses are JSON-parsed and may surface confusing errors
description: rpc() calls fetch then immediately does response.json() without checking response.ok. If the Sui RPC server returns a 502/503 (e.g., during sandbox restart), the response body is HTML, not JSON. response.json() throws SyntaxError: 'Unexpected token < in JSON at position 0'. This error reaches App.tsx's per-pool error banner verbatim — confusing and not actionable. Net behavior: the failure is surfaced (not silent), but the error text is misleading.
impact: Operator-facing error text quality during sandbox restart. Not a correctness bug — the failure is observable, just hard to diagnose.
recommendation: Add `if (!response.ok) throw new Error(\`${method} HTTP ${response.status}\`);` between fetch and json().

title: buildQueryEventsFn cursor advancement: cursor is passed but never advanced across pages
description:
buildQueryEventsFn returns a closure that issues a single suix_queryEvents call per invocation, accepting `cursor` from the caller (fillFetcher) and forwarding it to the RPC. fillFetcher.ts (line 77) does `cursor = response.nextCursor` to advance pagination. This works IF buildQueryEventsFn faithfully threads the cursor through to the RPC and returns the correct nextCursor. Let me verify: line 271 calls rpc with `[{ MoveModule: ... }, cursor, 50, true]`. Sui's suix_queryEvents accepts `cursor` as the second parameter — when cursor is null, it returns from the start (or, with descending=true, from newest); with a cursor, it returns events strictly older than that point. Iter-2 forwards cursor correctly. Returned `nextCursor: result.nextCursor ?? null` — correct. So pagination DOES advance.

However, there is still a subtle correctness issue: the queryEventsFn is built with closure over `(rpcUrl, packageId)` only. fillFetcher passes `{packageId, poolId, cursor}`, but buildQueryEventsFn IGNORES the passed packageId and poolId in favor of its closure's packageId. The closure's packageId comes from the per-pool fetchPoolStats invocation — which IS the same as descriptor.packageId... wait, packageId is global per-deployment, so this is fine. But poolId is poolId-specific, and buildQueryEventsFn does NOT pass poolId to the RPC filter (which is correct — module='pool' returns ALL pools). It is fillFetcher's job to filter by poolId post-hoc. So the design is consistent.

The real risk: the suix_queryEvents call returns ALL events from module='pool' for the entire deployed package. With multiple pools running, our 50-event page cap consumes mostly other-pool events for each per-pool fetch. fetchPoolStats is called once per pool, so we make N (=2-3) full event scans per refresh. This is wasteful but not a correctness bug. Filing as 'high' anyway because: if the sandbox has high event throughput on competing pools, our pool's 50-fill window may not fit in any reasonable number of pages, and fetchFills will paginate forever (bounded only by `hasNextPage: false`, which on a busy sandbox may be never).
impact: On a high-throughput sandbox where most events belong to other pools, fetchFills for our pool may issue dozens or hundreds of RPC calls per refresh tick before either of its stop conditions fires. The 20s refresh interval may be exceeded by the in-flight fetch.
recommendation: Add a hard pagination ceiling in fillFetcher (e.g. MAX_PAGES = 20). Or: restructure the data layer to issue one suix_queryEvents query per refresh and demultiplex events to all pools in a single pass, instead of per-pool. The latter is more invasive but matches the chain-shape note that the MoveModule filter returns all pools.

title: App polling effect re-fetches even when previous tick still in-flight; potential request stampede + state race
description: The polling useEffect runs setInterval(20s). Each tick fires Promise.allSettled over all pools. There is no guard against the previous tick still being in-flight: if a per-pool fetchPoolStats takes >20s (entirely possible during chain-shape-noted BigVector slice churn or a busy sandbox), tick N+1 starts before tick N's setState has committed. Both ticks resolve in arbitrary order; setState applies last-writer-wins, which may be the older request. The user can see stale data overwrite fresh data. There is also no abort signal — when the component unmounts mid-tick, the setState may still fire (mitigated by the cleanup `clearInterval` but no equivalent for in-flight promises).
impact: Sparkline freshness AC (AC1.5) is intermittently violated under slow/concurrent ticks: a slow fetch can overwrite a more recent fast fetch with stale data. Also a potential React 'Can't perform a state update on unmounted component' warning if unmount happens during a tick.
recommendation: Track a per-tick AbortController; call controller.abort() when the next tick starts or component unmounts. Alternatively, use a tick-id and only commit setState if the resolved tick is the latest.

title: Polling effect drops poolErrors history by re-setting state with only the latest tick's errors
description: Each polling tick computes poolErrors from THAT tick's settled results, then setState({status, cards, poolErrors}). Errors from previous ticks are dropped if the latest tick succeeds. This is intentional (you want the latest snapshot), but it also means transient errors are visible only for one tick window — if a card fails on tick N and succeeds on tick N+1, the user has 0-20 seconds to notice. For an actionability-focused error UX (the iter-1 H-9 concern), this is too brief. For the AC's structural compliance (an error UI exists), it is enough.
impact: Transient per-pool errors flash and disappear; the user may miss them entirely. Not a correctness bug; UX paper-cut.
recommendation: Keep a running error log in state with timestamps; render the most recent N or only those from the last 60 seconds. Alternatively: log to console.warn in addition to surfacing in the alert banner, so missed errors leave a trail.
